newRows.name: The Anglican Communion in the Twentieth Century
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), on the Lambeth and Anglican Consultative Council records and two standard histories. Its window opens in 1906, where the Victorian Church of England entry ends.

livingEvidence.basis: Settled on dated evidence. Settled on a verified 2022 report of a Lambeth Conference.
livingEvidence.evidence: Vatican News, 'Fifteenth Lambeth Conference kicks off in Canterbury' (July 2022): independent news; verified.
livingEvidence.grade: CD (Contemporary-Documented); newest dated item 2022, newest verified 2022

newRows.sourcing: Rich: the records of the Lambeth Conference and the Anglican Consultative Council. Two standard histories come from university presses, by Kevin Ward (2006) and William Sachs, ed. (2017).
newRows.floorNote: No question. In 1920 the bishops at Lambeth named the Nicene Creed as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith.
newRows.relationsSummary: It carries on from the Victorian Church of England and the Oxford Movement, whose entries end in 1906. Elsewhere in this era Anglicans appear inside other stories, such as the East African Revival and the Church of South India.
newRows.why: When Kevin Ward wrote his history in 2006, most Anglicans belonged to churches outside the West. Their bishops met in the Lambeth Conference. There they spoke on Christian unity, on limiting families and on sexuality.
newRows.teaser: A worldwide family of churches whose bishops met at Lambeth, and whose members came to live mostly outside the West.
newRows.longDescription: The bishops of the Anglican churches met in the Lambeth Conference, in 1920, 1930, 1968 and 1998 among other years. In 1920 they sent out an Appeal to All Christian People. It named the Scriptures, the Nicene Creed, the two sacraments and a shared ministry as the ground of a future unity. In 1930 they voted 193 to 67, with 47 not voting, on limiting or avoiding parenthood. Where a couple clearly felt a moral obligation to do so, they said, the method must be decided on Christian principles. Lambeth proposed an Anglican Consultative Council in 1968, and it first met at Limuru, Kenya, in 1971. Over the century most of the Communion came to live outside the West. In 1998 the bishops passed a resolution on human sexuality. In June 2008 the first Global Anglican Future Conference (GAFCON) met in Jerusalem and issued the Jerusalem Declaration.
newRows.legacy: By 2006, Kevin Ward found, most of its members belonged to churches outside the West. Ward and William Sachs both tell its twentieth century as one Communion's story.
voices: The Lambeth Conference of 1920 — whose Appeal to All Christian People named the Nicene Creed as the sufficient statement of the Christian faith
The Lambeth Conference of 1930 — whose resolution on limiting parenthood was the only one that year with a recorded vote
The Anglican Consultative Council — proposed at Lambeth in 1968, and first meeting at Limuru, Kenya, in 1971
The Global Anglican Future Conference — which met in Jerusalem in June 2008 and issued the Jerusalem Declaration

newRows.name: The Faith-Mission Movement in the Twentieth Century
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). It is a movement carried by mission agencies across many churches, not a church itself. Its window opens in 1917, when its agencies formed an association of their own.

livingEvidence.basis: A current, a label or a skeleton; the flag is a judgment on the evidence. The one dated item concerns a single agency that no item here ties to the movement.
livingEvidence.evidence: Christianity Today and Religion News Service, obituaries of George Verwer, founder of Operation Mobilisation (April 2023): independent news; verified. No item ties Operation Mobilisation to the movement, so this evidence is weak.
livingEvidence.grade: CD (Contemporary-Documented); newest dated item 2023, newest verified 2023

newRows.sourcing: Moderate: the association's records in the Wheaton College archives. Klaus Fiedler (1994) and William Svelmoe (2008) study it, inside wider histories by Joel Carpenter and Wilbert Shenk (1990) and Dana Robert (2009).
newRows.floorNote: Not yet assessed on a dated text. The movement has no confession of its own. It is assessed through the dated statements of the agencies that carried it, and none is cited here yet.
newRows.relationsSummary: It is one of two currents that came out of the Edinburgh conference of 1910; the other built the ecumenical movement. Its founders, the Wheaton archives record, no longer felt at one with that growing ecumenical movement.
newRows.why: In 1917 independent mission agencies formed a fellowship of their own, the Interdenominational Foreign Mission Association. Its members were popularly known as 'faith missions'. Klaus Fiedler tells their history as one movement, from Hudson Taylor to present-day Africa.
newRows.teaser: Mission societies with no denominational tie formed a fellowship of their own in 1917, and were popularly known as faith missions.
newRows.longDescription: In 1917 leaders of independent mission agencies met in March and again in September. From these meetings came the Interdenominational Foreign Mission Association, 'a fellowship of missions without denominational affiliation'. Its archives describe founders who no longer felt at one with the growing ecumenical movement. Its member missions were popularly known as faith missions. Under the faith principle, a mission looked to prayer alone for its support. By 1965 the association counted forty-six missions. Wycliffe Bible Translators grew from the same culture. Its training began at Camp Wycliffe, which W. Cameron Townsend and L. L. Legters founded in Arkansas in 1934. Over time, William Svelmoe shows, the faith principle gave way to more open fundraising. Klaus Fiedler tells the whole story as one movement, from Hudson Taylor to present-day Africa.
newRows.legacy: Klaus Fiedler's history of 1994 carries the movement's story from Hudson Taylor into present-day Africa.
voices: The Interdenominational Foreign Mission Association — 'a fellowship of missions without denominational affiliation', organized in 1917
Arthur F. Glasser — whose 1965 account in Christianity Today records the association's forty-six missions and their popular name
W. Cameron Townsend and L. L. Legters — who founded Camp Wycliffe in Arkansas in 1934 to train Bible translators

newRows.name: The Rescue Mission Movement
newRows.region: New York, then the U.S. and Canada
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1906, when mission leaders in New York formed a federation of gospel missions. Its first missions are older, from 1872, and are told here as its beginning.

livingEvidence.basis: A current, a label or a skeleton; the flag is a judgment on the evidence. Its present network describes itself as a movement.
livingEvidence.evidence: Citygate Network press release (8 October 2024), describing itself as 'a movement of nearly 300 rescue missions and faith-based organizations': own voice; verified as reported in a search result.
livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2024, newest verified 2024

newRows.sourcing: Moderate: one academic study, Norris Magnuson's Salvation in the Slums (1977). The network's own history, a 1972 history in Christianity Today and the Billy Graham Center Archives add to it.
newRows.floorNote: Not yet assessed on a dated text. Its network keeps a statement of faith, but the text and its first date are not cited here.
newRows.relationsSummary: The Salvation Army did the same kind of work, but as a church body. Norris Magnuson places the rescue missions among the revivalist welfare movements of 1865 to 1920.
newRows.why: In 1872 Jerry McAuley opened a mission on Water Street in New York. Others followed, and in 1906 mission leaders in New York formed a federation of gospel missions. A historian places them among the revivalist welfare movements of 1865 to 1920.
newRows.teaser: City gospel missions, from New York's Water Street in 1872 to a union of missions in 1913.
newRows.longDescription: In 1872 Jerry McAuley opened a mission on Water Street in New York. Others followed. In 1877 Colonel George Clarke and his wife Sarah opened the Pacific Garden Mission in Chicago, apparently without ties to McAuley. It aimed to be 'a harbor for wrecked and ruined lives'. In 1906 mission leaders in New York formed a National Federation of Gospel Missions. On 17 September 1913 a wider body followed, the International Union of Gospel Missions, with about fifty missions. The historian Norris Magnuson counts the rescue missions among the revivalist welfare movements of 1865 to 1920. Their welfare work, he argues, came from a commitment to evangelism and personal holiness. By 1972 the union counted some 350 members. In 2000 it became the Association of Gospel Rescue Missions.
newRows.legacy: The union, renamed the Association of Gospel Rescue Missions in 2000, was still the movement's network in 2010.

Colonel George Clarke and Sarah Clarke — who opened the Pacific Garden Mission in Chicago in 1877
Sidney Whittemore — who led the International Union of Gospel Missions at its founding in 1913

newRows.name: The Christian Homeschool Movement
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in March 1983, when the Home School Legal Defense Association was launched. The Christian day schools and a book of 1975 came before it and are told here as background. It covers only the Christian root of homeschooling that Mitchell Stevens names, not the movement as a whole.

livingEvidence.basis: A current, a label or a skeleton; the flag is a judgment on the evidence. One carrier is still active; no dated item speaks for the Christian wing as a whole.
livingEvidence.evidence: Michael Farris, 'A Tribute to Dr. James Dobson', HSLDA (21 August 2025): own voice; verified. Reason (19 November 2025), on homeschooling's growth in 2024-25: independent news, not specific to Christian homeschooling; verified.
livingEvidence.grade: CR (Contemporary-Reported); newest dated item 2025, newest verified 2025

newRows.sourcing: Moderate: three university-press studies, by Mitchell Stevens (2001), Milton Gaither (2008) and Alan Peshkin (1986), and the carriers' own texts.
newRows.floorNote: Not yet assessed on a dated text. Its legal defense association calls itself a Christian organization, but no dated statement of faith is cited here.
newRows.relationsSummary: The school Alan Peshkin studied was a fundamentalist Baptist one, which ties this entry to Fundamentalism. Mitchell Stevens traces a second, liberal root of homeschooling, which is not Christian and stays outside this entry.
newRows.why: Sociologist Mitchell Stevens found that homeschooling was not a scatter of private choices but an organized movement. He traced one of its two roots to the Christian day-school movement of the 1960s and 1970s. A legal defense association for homeschooling families followed in 1983.
newRows.teaser: In 1983 two homeschooling fathers, both lawyers, founded a legal defense association for families who taught their children at home.
newRows.longDescription: Sociologist Mitchell Stevens traces one root of homeschooling to the Christian day-school movement of the 1960s and 1970s. Alan Peshkin spent eighteen months in one such school, a Baptist school in Illinois, in the late 1970s. He called it a 'total world'. Raymond and Dorothy Moore's Better Late Than Early (1975) argued that formal lessons should wait until a child was older. Around 1982 James Dobson interviewed Raymond Moore about the book on the air. Some families who heard the broadcast began to teach their children at home. In March 1983 two homeschooling fathers, the lawyers Michael Farris and J. Michael Smith, launched the Home School Legal Defense Association with their wives. At the time, homeschooling was legal in only a handful of states. A reviewer of Stevens's study summed the movement up as 'a woman's enterprise, in which men are usually junior partners'.
newRows.legacy: By 2001 Mitchell Stevens could describe homeschooling as 'an elaborate social movement'.

newRows.name: The Liturgical Movement
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window closes in 1962, where historians close the Catholic movement, at the Second Vatican Council. The parish after the Council is told in its own entry.

livingEvidence.basis: A closed tradition. Its history closes at the Council, and the entry on the parish after 1962 carries what followed.
livingEvidence.evidence: Societas Liturgica, Newsletter 51 (Autumn 2025): a society for liturgical study and renewal, alive today; own voice; verified. It is not counted as the movement itself.
livingEvidence.grade: n/a (flag false on a documented end)

newRows.sourcing: Rich: its own journal from 1926 and its English handbooks of 1935 and 1937. Two academic histories, by Keith Pecklers (1998) and by John Fenwick and Bryan Spinks (1995), tell its story.
newRows.floorNote: No question. Its carriers were Catholic Benedictine houses and Anglican parishes, in churches that confess the Nicene Creed.
newRows.relationsSummary: It ran through Benedictine abbeys, journals and parishes rather than through the Vatican. The entry on the Catholic Church before the Council names it once, and the entry on the parish after the Council receives its outcome.
newRows.why: Historians date the popular liturgical movement from an address at Malines, Belgium, in 1909. It reached America through Saint John's Abbey in Collegeville, where the journal Orate Fratres was founded in 1926. In England, Gabriel Hebert's books gave the Parish Communion movement its handbook.
newRows.teaser: From a 1909 address in Malines, a movement for the renewal of worship reached Catholic abbeys and Anglican parishes.
newRows.longDescription: In 1909 Dom Lambert Beauduin spoke at the National Congress of Catholic Action in Malines, Belgium. Historians date the popular liturgical movement from that address. In 1926 Virgil Michel of Saint John's Abbey in Minnesota founded the journal Orate Fratres, the movement's voice. He also set up the Liturgical Press. Keith Pecklers has shown how closely its American leaders tied worship to social justice in the 1930s and 1940s. In England, Gabriel Hebert published Liturgy and Society in 1935. The Church Times later called it 'the Bible of the Parish Communion Movement'. Hebert's collection The Parish Communion (1937) set out a practice that changed the pattern of Sunday-morning worship.
newRows.legacy: John Fenwick and Bryan Spinks tell its story across Catholic, Anglican, Eastern and North American churches, and close the Catholic part in 1962.
voices: Dom Lambert Beauduin — whose address at Malines in 1909 historians take as the movement's start
Virgil Michel — who founded the journal Orate Fratres at Saint John's Abbey in 1926
Gabriel Hebert — whose Liturgy and Society (1935) was called 'the Bible of the Parish Communion Movement'

newRows.name: The Third Wave & the Vineyard
newRows.informalName: The Vineyard and the Third Wave
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1982, when the Signs and Wonders course began at Fuller Seminary. The entry on the charismatic renewal and the Jesus movement closes where this one begins.

livingEvidence.basis: A current, a label or a skeleton; the flag is a judgment on the evidence. The newest dated item is an ethnography of living Vineyard churches.
livingEvidence.evidence: Jon Bialecki, A Diagram for Fire (University of California Press, 2017), an ethnography of Vineyard churches: independent scholarship; verified.
livingEvidence.grade: CD (Contemporary-Documented); newest dated item 2017, newest verified 2017

newRows.sourcing: Rich: Fuller Seminary's archive of the course, its founders' books, Fuller's own study of it and four academic studies.
newRows.floorNote: Not yet assessed on a verified dated text. The Vineyard churches' statement of faith has not yet been checked against its publisher's own text.
newRows.relationsSummary: It follows the charismatic renewal and the Jesus movement, whose entry closes where this one begins, in 1982. The Toronto Blessing of 1994 grew inside one of its churches.
newRows.why: In 1982 John Wimber began teaching 'Signs and Wonders' at Fuller Seminary. C. Peter Wagner called the stream 'the Third Wave'. Its people sought the gifts of the Spirit without taking on Pentecostal or charismatic theology or worship styles.
newRows.teaser: A seminary course called 'Signs and Wonders', and a stream of churches that sought the Spirit's gifts without becoming Pentecostal.
newRows.longDescription: In 1982 John Wimber and C. Peter Wagner began teaching MC510, 'Signs and Wonders', at Fuller Theological Seminary in Pasadena. The course ran until 1985 and drew controversy. Fuller's faculty dropped it in early 1986 and published its own study, Ministry and the Miraculous, in 1987. Wagner called the stream 'the Third Wave'. Its people believed in the power and gifts of the Holy Spirit without adopting Pentecostal or charismatic theology or worship styles. Wimber set out his method in Power Evangelism in 1985. In 1994 a revival called the Toronto Blessing began at the Toronto Airport Vineyard. The Vineyard association cut its ties with that church in December 1995. Margaret Poloma published a study of the revival in 1997. Jon Bialecki has since studied 'the Third Wave' by name, and the Vineyard as 'an American charismatic movement'.
newRows.legacy: Donald Miller studied the Vineyard in 1997 beside two other new church networks, and Jon Bialecki's ethnography of it followed in 2017.

newRows.name: Promise Keepers & the Christian Men's Movement
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1990, when Promise Keepers began. The size of its 1997 gathering in Washington is a crowd estimate.

livingEvidence.basis: A current, a label or a skeleton; the flag is a judgment on the evidence. The ministry that carried it held a large rally after 2010.
livingEvidence.evidence: K-LOVE News, report of the Promise Keepers event at AT&T Stadium, Arlington, Texas (16 July 2021), nearly 30,000 men: independent broadcaster; verified.
livingEvidence.grade: CD (Contemporary-Documented); newest dated item 2021, newest verified 2021

newRows.sourcing: Moderate: a university-press study by John Bartkowski (2004), an encyclopedia entry, the movement's own book of 1994 and dated contemporary reporting.
newRows.floorNote: No question, on a reported text. In 1997 a newspaper reported its statement of faith. It named one God in three persons, the deity of Jesus, and salvation through his death.
newRows.relationsSummary: Megachurches and Lausanne-era evangelicals shared its evangelical setting but not its subject. James Mathisen set it apart from the wider men's movement of the same decade.
newRows.why: In 1990 a college football coach and a friend started a ministry, and its first men called themselves Promise Keepers. Within six years it filled 22 stadiums with nearly 1.2 million men. Each man made seven promises about friendship with other men, purity, marriage, and reaching across racial and denominational barriers.
newRows.teaser: A football coach's 1990 idea that filled stadiums with men making seven promises, and reached Washington in 1997.
newRows.longDescription: On 20 March 1990, Bill McCartney, the University of Colorado football coach, drove with a friend from Boulder to Pueblo. From that trip grew a group of about seventy men who called themselves Promise Keepers. In 1991, 4,200 men met at the university's basketball arena. In 1996, 22 stadium rallies drew nearly 1.2 million men. Each man made seven promises, published in 1994 as Seven Promises of a Promise Keeper. They pledged purity, strong marriages, and friendship across racial and denominational barriers. On 4 October 1997 a crowd estimated at about a million men gathered in Washington, D.C., for Stand in the Gap. In March 1998 the ministry began laying off 345 paid staff. Sociologist John Bartkowski later traced the rise and fall of this Christian men's movement.
newRows.legacy: In 2001 James Mathisen called it 'the decade's most unexpected and immediately successful movement within the American church'.

registerEdits.old: Iglesia ni Cristo was registered in the Philippines on 27 July 1914. Its own history presented Felix Manalo as God's messenger for the last days. Its magazine Pasugo carried its teaching from February 1939. In 2010, by its own counts, it was the largest church founded in the Philippines. No independent count is cited here.
registerEdits.new: Iglesia ni Cristo, 'the Church of Christ', was registered with the government of the Philippines on 27 July 1914. It was registered under Felix Y. Manalo, and its own history presents him as God's messenger for the last days. It honored Jesus as Lord and Savior but taught that he was not God. From February 1939 its magazine Pasugo, in Tagalog and English, set out that teaching. It passed through two changes of leader, in 1963 and 2009. By its own counts it was, by 2010, the largest church founded in the Philippines. No independent count is cited here, and independent scholarship on the church is thin.
